query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Mo content to x = 1 in the CoCrFeNiMox-based composite will foster the formation of a denser, continuous oxide-molybdate glaze at high temperatures due to enhanced FCC lattice distortion and σ-phase formation, thereby reducing friction and wear across the full temperature range compared to the Mo0.2 baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox high-entropy-alloy matrix powder (with x = 0.2 as baseline), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2 composite powder, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3, subsequently sintered by SPS.
generation.intervention: Increase the Mo content in the high-entropy alloy matrix from x = 0.2 (baseline) to x = 1 during powder mixing and SPS processing.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering under vacuum at 40 MPa with heating to 1250 °C (150 °C/min, 3 min hold) followed by furnace cooling; tribological tests using a ball-on-disk setup in air with a 6 mm Si3N4 ball, 8 N load, 4 mm rotation radius, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and a total sliding distance of 270 m at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced Mo content leads to increased FCC lattice distortion and promotes the formation of a hard Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase, with Ag, Ni/MoS2, and Cr2O3 remaining at matrix boundaries to facilitate film formation.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the increased Mo provides solid-solution and second-phase strengthening that suppress plastic deformation and scratching, while at high temperatures Mo assists in tribochemical reactions that yield layered silver molybdates and oxides. The compaction of these products forms a dense glaze, which effectively separates the sliding surfaces and reduces interfacial shear, yielding lower friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Mo0.2 composite, the Mo1 composite is expected to exhibit improved wear resistance and a more robust, continuous glaze at 800 °C, leading to lower wear rates and friction coefficients especially in the high-temperature regime. Some variations in friction behavior may occur at intermediate temperatures, but overall, a better strength/wear balance is anticipated.
generation.baseline: The Mo0.2 composite, characterized by predominantly an FCC solid solution with minimal σ phase, a friction coefficient of ~0.66 at room temperature (peaking at ~0.75 at 200 °C and dropping to ~0.21 at 800 °C), and wear rates ranging from 13.1×10^-6 mm³/N·m (room temperature) to 98.1×10^-6 mm³/N·m (400 °C).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under dry sliding in air using a Si3N4 counterface, with the specified load (8 N), sliding speed (0.15 m/s), test distance (270 m), and temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C). Results may differ under alternative environmental or loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of performance improvements (in terms of friction reduction and wear rate) is uncertain due to potential sensitivities in σ-phase development, glaze continuity, and processing variabilities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of composites with Mo contents corresponding to x = 0.2 (baseline), 0.5, and 1 under identical SPS conditions. Conduct ball-on-disk tribological tests at room temperature, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C. Use XRD to assess lattice distortion and detect σ-phase formation; SEM/EDS and Raman spectroscopy to characterize the microstructure and glaze formation on wear tracks; and measure friction coefficients, wear rates, and hardness.
measurements: XRD for phase identification and lattice distortion analysis
SEM/EDS for mapping of σ-phase and glaze distributions
Vickers hardness and compression stress–strain tests
Profilometry-derived wear scar dimensions and calculated wear rates
Raman spectroscopy for identifying oxide/molybdate glaze components
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo1 composite does not exhibit a significantly denser and more continuous oxide-molybdate glaze at high temperature (800 °C) and fails to show reduced friction and wear performance compared to the Mo0.2 baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
